item.title: History, mathematics and physics: two cases of the inverse square law
item.description: arXiv:2611.16700v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: How did mathematicians of the past relate to history? What can we learn from their experience? It is a truism to say that all people are embedded in history. It impacts on them in ways that they may or may not realise. At the two extremes, some may be completely oblivious; others may deliberately set out to change the historical narrative and the course of history. In this chapter, I explore these questions through two case studies. Both are of eminent British mathematicians/physicists in the late 1800s and their handling of an inverse square law of force. Both case studies show ways in which these men were blind to the history of their subject, conscious of it but limited by it, or deliberately trying to use it. First, I look at William Thomson's and James Clerk Maxwell's attempts to establish the inverse square law of electrostatics in the 1850s to 1870s. I ask the question, why did Maxwell devote the last years of his life to editing the 100-year-old electrical researches of Henry Cavendish and repeating Cavendish's experimental verification of the inverse square law of electrostatic repulsion? Second, I discuss John Henry Poynting and Newton's law of gravitation in the 1880s and 1890s, asking why Poynting preferred to describe his experiments as measurements of the mean density of the Earth rather than of the gravitational constant.

item.title: Arnold's problem on paper folding
item.description: arXiv:1004.0545v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: This is a story about the question of whether folding a square flat can increase its perimeter. It is written primarily for school students.

item.title: The D'Alembert-Lagrange Principle and Lagrange Equations
item.description: arXiv:2607.24825v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In this expository-research article we present a rigorous geometric framework for analytical mechanics in the extended phase space, accommodating general constraints that may be non-linear in velocities. We prove that the space of virtual displacements and ideal constraint reactions depend strictly on the intrinsic geometry of the constraint manifold and are entirely invariant under the choice of analytical constraint equations. Furthermore, we show that the Lagrange equations of the second kind are derived through the covector covariance of the variational derivative operator under the embedding mapping of the configuration manifold.
item.dc:creator: Oleg Zubelevich

item.title: Ehrhart Properties under Operations on Lattice Polytopes
item.description: arXiv:2610.06338v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: This paper investigates the preservation of three classes of Ehrhart properties under various operations on lattice polytopes. These operations include Cartesian products, lattice joins, lattice pyramids, free sums, Minkowski sums, Cayley sums, reflexive polarity, and integral dilations. Specifically, we consider the following properties frequently studied in Ehrhart theory: (i): Positivity of Ehrhart coefficients, including Ehrhart positivity and magic positivity. In particular, we present lattice point counting formulas for the polytopes generated by these operations. (ii): Coefficient properties of the $h^*$-polynomial, including symmetry, unimodality, log-concavity, ultra log-concavity, real-rootedness, and $\gamma$-positivity. (iii): Geometric properties, including the spanning property, the integer decomposition property, very ampleness, and the existence of unimodular triangulation, regular unimodular triangulation, and quadratic triangulation. We determine which properties are preserved under these eight operations, establishing preservation theorems or constructing explicit counterexamples. Furthermore, when a property is not preserved in general, we investigate sufficient or equivalent conditions for its preservation.
item.dc:creator: Feihu Liu

item.title: The Gleason--Kahane--Zelazko theorem: a gentle introduction
item.description: arXiv:2610.39769v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: After some personal recollections of Jean-Pierre Kahane, this paper gives a gentle introduction to the Gleason-Kahane-Zelazko theorem. The theorem states that a normalised complex-linear functional on a unital complex Banach algebra is multiplicative whenever it does not vanish on invertible elements. Neither continuity of the functional nor commutativity of the algebra is assumed. We give a detailed account of three proofs: the original argument of Gleason and, independently, Kahane and Zelazko; the polynomial proof of Roitman and Sternfeld; and a proof by the author. We explain the complex analysis behind each: a special case of Hadamard's factorisation theorem, a polynomial argument using the fundamental theorem of algebra, and the Polya-Saxer theorem on zero-free entire functions and their derivatives. The elementary entire-function lemma needed for the first proof is proved in full; the Polya-Saxer theorem is used without proof. We give full details of the algebraic argument common to the three proofs, which deduces multiplicativity from the preservation of squares, including the non-commutative case. We then discuss applications and counterexamples, and present an extension to Ransford's generalised spectra using the Roitman--Sternfeld argument. We conclude with a brief guide to the more recent literature.
